analysis.one_liner: Makes a tax break for business owners permanent and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee after Representative Biggs introduced it with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make a large tax deduction for business owners permanent, cut the top rate on business income to the corporate rate of 21 percent by nearly doubling the deduction, remove the limits that currently tie the deduction to wages paid and exclude doctors, lawyers, and other professionals, shield corporate restructurings from tax when ownership does not change, and repeal the estate tax that applies to very large inheritances. It would also keep 'step-up' basis, which wipes out capital gains tax on inherited assets. Nothing happened after its introduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of pass-through businesses — including law firms, hedge funds, and other professional practices — and wealthy heirs. The expanded deduction plus the repeal of the estate tax concentrates the gains at the top, since most pass-through income goes to high earners and only estates above the multimillion-dollar exemption owe estate tax.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the 20 percent deduction for qualified business income permanent, a break that was scheduled to expire after 2025.

Nearly doubles the deduction from 20 to 43 percent (47 percent after 2025), which the bill text says is designed to bring the top rate on business income down to 21 percent, matching the corporate rate.

Removes the cap that ties the deduction to wages paid and repeals the exclusion for 'specified service' businesses like law, medicine, and consulting, so high-income professionals who are now excluded become eligible.
Repeals the estate tax for deaths after 2019 while retaining step-up basis, which means large inheritances escape capital gains tax as well.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury. These are unreimbursed tax cuts, so the cost shows up either as a larger deficit or as higher taxes on someone else in the future. Wage earners — who cannot claim the business deduction and whose payroll taxes are untouched — would bear the largest share of any replacement burden, though the bill does not specify offsetting cuts.

drawbacks.text: The expanded deduction and estate tax repeal reduce federal revenue substantially; the Joint Committee on Taxation has estimated repeal of the estate tax alone at roughly $100–$150 billion per decade, and the bill text does not identify any offsetting revenue.

Extending full eligibility to high-income professional service firms would allow top-bracket earners (currently 37 percent) to pay an effective rate near 21 percent, and Treasury and academic analyses of the deduction have flagged income-shifting from wages into pass-through income as a key abuse, which the bill would make more profitable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are real for business owners and heirs, and a lower rate on small firms can simplify filing and free up cash for hiring or investment. But the design favors the top heavily: most pass-through income already flows to households in the top 1 percent, the estate tax touches only multimillion-dollar estates, and the cost to the deficit is large. As a package aimed at 'small business', it delivers more to large partnerships and wealthy families than to the corner store.

outcome.mechanism: Representative Biggs introduced the bill in late October 2019 and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up; it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 31, 2019, and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history; the bill died in committee at the end of the 116th Congress.
No other member cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody won a policy change, but the status quo was preserved. Business owners and wealthy families kept the existing deduction structure and estate tax rather than the more generous versions the bill would have created, while the federal government avoided the associated revenue loss.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; no change resulted

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote occurred.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a solo Republican effort with no cosponsors from either party and never advanced.

industries.industry: Owners of pass-through businesses (law firms, partnerships, S corporations)
industries.note: The bill would nearly double their deduction, remove the wage cap, and open eligibility to high-income professional service firms, lowering their top rate toward 21 percent. The cost is borne by the broader tax base.
Estate tax repeal plus retained step-up basis means very large inheritances would owe neither estate tax nor capital gains tax. Only estates above the multimillion-dollar exemption are affected.
The provisions reduce revenue with no identified offsets, raising the deficit or forcing future tax increases elsewhere.
